title: Random pushes escape in bf16 too
caption: The random-push escapes of iteration 4 under four numerics built from one bf16 snapshot of Qwen3-8B, at the absolute displacement, directions and common-random-number slots of iteration 4. Left: share of 40 fixed random directions that escape at alpha 2, each engine scored against its own twin, with Wilson 95% intervals (W8A16 on connected components is the screen-level value, because its confirmation stage was incomplete). Right: per-sample plan noise at alpha 2, valid attempts on a catalogue alternative to the default out of 50. bf16 escapes on almost the same directions as the 8-bit W8A8 engine, and activation rounding alone (W16A8) adds nothing. The bf16 plan-noise cell of iteration 5 on connected components (1 of 50, grey marker) used the ban-free unit and other direction seeds; this control did not separate the two.

Both panels share the x-axis categories 'connected components' and 'shortest path' and four bars per category in this legend order and colour: 'W8A8 (8-bit floating-point weights and activations)' dark red, 'W8A16 (8-bit floating-point weights, bf16 activations)' orange, 'W16A8 (bf16 weights, 8-bit floating-point activations)' light blue, 'bf16' dark blue. Panel A (left), title 'Escape fraction of 40 fixed random directions, alpha 2', y-axis label 'escape fraction (share of 40 directions)', range 0 to 1, bars with Wilson 95% error bars. Values: connected components: W8A8 0.725 (29/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.5717 to 0.8389); W8A16 0.7 (28/40 at the screen level, because its confirmation stage was incomplete; draw this bar hatched with no error bar and annotate it 'screen level'); W16A8 0.6 (24/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.4460 to 0.7365); bf16 0.65 (26/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.4951 to 0.7787). shortest path: W8A8 0.2 (8/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.1050 to 0.3476); W8A16 0.125 (5/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.0546 to 0.2611); W16A8 0.15 (6/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.0706 to 0.2907); bf16 0.15 (6/40; Wilson 95% interval 0.0706 to 0.2907). Values: connected components: W8A8 30/50 = 0.6; W8A16 27/50 = 0.54; W16A8 22/50 = 0.44; bf16 25/50 = 0.5. shortest path: W8A8 22/50 = 0.44; W8A16 19/50 = 0.38; W16A8 18/50 = 0.36; bf16 22/50 = 0.44. In panel B draw a short grey horizontal tick over the connected components group at 0.02 labelled 'iteration 5: bf16, ban-free unit, other seeds (1/50)'. Print each value above its bar. summary: At the same absolute dose, bf16 reproduces the 8-bit escape fractions and plan-noise rates; 8-bit floating-point activation rounding adds nothing.

title: Where the substitute of a ban is carried
caption: Stage A in bf16 Qwen3-8B: transfer of the substitute Y of the ban (Y share under the cell minus that of the neutral twin, N = 30 paired slots per cell) when the residual states of the full ban prompt are exchanged into the neutral twin at a block band of the task-specification positions, when the key-value cache of the condition span is spliced in, or when the read position is exchanged at all blocks. The task-specification states carry the ban on shortest path and kth smallest; the condition span carries it on two sum and find duplicate; on the grid task each carries part of it; the read position carries nothing on any task. Matched-norm random exchanges and a placebo twin transfer at most 0.13.

title: Steering the fork of Gemma toward BFS
caption: Edits at the fork position (response index 32, layer 22) of gemma-3-4b-it on the grid task, N = 50 paired slots per cell. An SAE clamp sets the k Gemma Scope 2 latents that best separate forced-BFS from forced-DFS prompts to their BFS-class mean; difference-in-means and random-latent edits are scaled to the clamp's norm or matched on its effect on the fork log-odds. Bars give programs attempting BFS and programs that are BFS and pass the hidden tests; the line gives the pass rate. The SAE clamp moves the plan, difference in means at the same norm moves it further, and every edit toward the minority algorithm costs correctness; DAS at rank 4 makes every program BFS and none correct.
image_gen_detailed_description: Grouped bar chart with a line on a secondary axis. X-axis categories in this order: 'twin (no edit)'; 'SAE clamp, top 5 input-selected latents'; 'SAE clamp, top 20 input-selected latents'; 'SAE clamp, top 50 input-selected latents'; '50 random latents (top-50 norm)'; 'difference in means (top-20 norm)'; 'difference in means (top-50 norm)'; 'difference in means matched on effect (top-20 level)'; 'difference in means matched on effect (top-50 level)'; 'SAE clamp, top 20 output-scored latents'; 'DAS rank-4 interchange'. Two bar series on the left y-axis 'programs out of 50' (range 0 to 50): 'attempted BFS' (light blue) values in category order 13, 18, 30, 36, 21, 46, 49, 32, 34, 25, 50; 'BFS and correct' (dark blue) values 6, 10, 9, 10, 9, 12, 7, 13, 14, 14, 0. Line series 'pass rate' on the right y-axis (range 0 to 1), red markers joined by a thin red line, values in category order 0.84, 0.84, 0.58, 0.48, 0.76, 0.32, 0.16, 0.62, 0.60, 0.78, 0.00. Draw a dashed horizontal reference line at 13 on the left axis labelled 'twin attempted BFS'. Rotate the x labels by 30 degrees and print each bar's value above it. What the reader must see: attempted BFS rises with the strength of the edit while correct BFS stays between 6 and 14 and the pass rate falls, down to 0 for DAS.
summary: Gemma's BFS-or-DFS fork is steerable by SAE latents and more so by difference in means, but every edit toward BFS breaks programs.

title: An NLA names the algorithm only where the prompt does
caption: Natural language autoencoder explanations of layer-20 states of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, judged blind, at three positions: on the token of the algorithm's name inside the condition sentence, at the end of that sentence (2 to 8 tokens later), and at the end of the prompt (about 170 tokens later, the preregistered readout). At the first two positions each state counts by the majority of three explanations (75 forced and 35 ban states); at the end of the prompt the shares count single explanations (8 of 1,080 forced and 3 of 420 ban explanations mention the algorithm). Explanations mention the algorithm and respect a ban's negation at the name token, and the identity fades within one sentence. Exploratory local control.
image_gen_detailed_description: Grouped bar chart. X-axis categories (positions) in this order: 'at the algorithm's name', 'end of that sentence (2 to 8 tokens later)', 'end of the prompt (about 170 tokens later)'. Four bar series with values in position order: 'forced prompt: mentions Y' (dark green) 0.8000 (60/75), 0.2667 (20/75), 0.0074 (8/1080); 'forced prompt: names Y as planned' (light green) 0.4800 (36/75), 0.1067 (8/75), 0 (0/1080); 'ban prompt: mentions the banned default' (dark orange) 0.8857 (31/35), 0.0571 (2/35), 0.0071 (3/420); 'ban prompt: names the default as planned' (light orange) 0.0571 (2/35), 0 (0/35), 0 (0/420). Y-axis label 'share of states (first two positions) or of explanations (end of the prompt)', range 0 to 1. Print each value above its bar with two decimals. What the reader must see: high mention rates at the name token, near zero one sentence later and at the end of the prompt.
summary: The NLA verbalises algorithm identity at the token that names it and loses it within a sentence; pre-code states name no algorithm.

title: Base-model variety against nudge movability
caption: Corrected in iteration 6 to compare like with like. The base model's off-default share among correct programs (beta) against the escape fraction of fixed random directions measured in bf16 at iteration 5's ban-free unit (mean of alpha 1 and 2), for the 15 existing tasks (filled blue circles; open grey circles joined by a segment mark iteration 4's 8-bit screen value of the same task) and the 15 new units (orange diamonds; the two reserve units hollow). Spearman: existing tasks 0.59 (one-sided permutation p 0.010, Bonett-Wright 95% interval 0.06 to 0.86), 0.79 with the 8-bit screen values; new units 0.15 (p 0.315, interval -0.44 to 0.65), 0.01 with the reserve units; pooled bf16 0.48 (p 0.005). The existing-task correlation is carried by tasks with low beta that never move. Section 6.3 shows that the ban-free unit moves fewer programs than iteration 4's absolute unit.
